description: Analysis and design of feedback control systems: modelling physical systems, transfer functions and block diagrams, transient and steady-state response, stability, root locus, Bode and Nyquist methods, PID tuning, state-space design and digital control. Every plant and controller is simulated in the browser, so students tune a controller and immediately see its step response, root locus and frequency response move.
modelledOn: Franklin, Powell and Emami-Naeini, Feedback Control of Dynamic Systems
Dorf and Bishop, Modern Control Systems
outcomes: Model electrical, mechanical and electromechanical systems as differential equations, transfer functions and state-space equations.
Reduce block diagrams and signal-flow graphs and determine transient response, steady-state error and stability.
Design compensators with the root locus and with Bode and Nyquist frequency-response methods to meet time- and frequency-domain specifications.
Design and tune PID controllers and explain integral windup, derivative filtering and practical tuning rules.
Design state-feedback controllers and observers, and implement controllers digitally with appropriate sampling.

units.title: Introduction to feedback control
topics: Open-loop and closed-loop control; the benefits and costs of feedback
The control design process: specifications, model, design, simulation, implementation
Laplace transform review for control
Examples: water-tank level, room temperature, and a hydroelectric generator speed governor holding grid frequency at 50 Hz

units.title: Modelling dynamic systems
topics: Electrical networks and operational amplifier circuits
Mechanical translational and rotational systems; gears and inertia reflection
Electromechanical systems: the armature-controlled DC motor
Thermal and fluid systems; electrical analogies
Linearisation of non-linear systems about an operating point
Identifying model parameters from measured step responses

units.title: Transfer functions and block diagrams
topics: Transfer functions, poles and zeros; from differential equations to transfer functions
Block diagram algebra and reduction
Signal-flow graphs and Mason's gain formula
Effects of feedback: sensitivity to parameter variation, disturbance rejection, noise

units.title: Time response, stability and steady-state error
topics: First-order response and the time constant
Second-order response: damping ratio, natural frequency, rise time, peak time, percentage overshoot, settling time
Higher-order systems and dominant poles; effect of zeros
Routh-Hurwitz stability criterion, including special cases
Steady-state error, system type and static error constants
Specifying performance for a solar-powered irrigation pump

units.title: Root locus
topics: The root locus: angle and magnitude conditions
Sketching rules: asymptotes, breakaway and break-in points, imaginary-axis crossings, angles of departure
Gain selection to meet transient specifications
Lead, lag and lead-lag compensator design on the root locus
Root contours and parameter sensitivity

units.title: Frequency response: Bode and Nyquist
topics: Frequency response and asymptotic Bode magnitude and phase plots
The Nyquist plot and the Nyquist stability criterion
Gain and phase margins; relation to transient response
Closed-loop frequency response and bandwidth; Nichols chart in brief
Lead, lag and lead-lag design in the frequency domain
Effect of time delay on stability, as in remote or networked control

units.title: PID controller design and tuning
topics: Proportional, integral and derivative actions and their effect on response
Practical PID: integral windup and anti-windup, derivative filtering, set-point weighting, bumpless transfer
Tuning methods: Ziegler-Nichols, Cohen-Coon and IMC-based tuning
Cascade and feedforward control
Tuning a DC motor speed loop and a battery charge controller on the simulator

units.title: State-space models
topics: State variables; converting between transfer functions and state-space forms
Solution of the state equation and the state-transition matrix
Controllability and observability
State feedback and pole placement; Ackermann's formula
Full-order observer design and the separation principle
The linear quadratic regulator in brief

units.title: Digital control
topics: Sampled-data systems and the zero-order hold; z-domain transfer functions
Discretising controllers: forward, backward and Tustin approximations
Stability in the z-plane and the Jury test
Implementing a digital PID on a microcontroller: sampling-rate choice, quantisation and computational delay
Grid frequency control and load shedding as a large-scale control problem

schedule.title: Feedback and control basics
schedule.exercise: Sketch block diagrams for a water-tank level loop and a room thermostat, labelling reference, error, controller, plant, sensor and disturbance.

tasks.title: Plot the step response of a heater with and without feedback for a 5 degree set-point change and compare final value and settling
Use the maths lab to find the Laplace transforms of five common signals and check each by inverting back to time
Model a hydro generator speed governor as a first-order lag with a load disturbance, and tune a gain to hold 50 Hz within 0.2 Hz

schedule.title: Modelling physical systems
schedule.exercise: Derive the differential equation for an RC circuit and a mass-spring-damper by hand, then state the analogy that links them.

tasks.title: Derive and plot the step response of an RC low-pass circuit with R of 10 kilohms and C of 10 microfarads, marking the time constant
Write the armature-controlled DC motor equations, combine them into one transfer function, and simulate its speed after a 12 V step
Reflect load inertia and friction through a gear train to the motor shaft, then predict and verify the new time constant by simulation

schedule.title: Linearisation and system identification
schedule.exercise: Explain in writing why a linear model is valid only near an operating point, and give one example from a tank with a square-root outflow.

tasks.title: Build the thermal model of a small oven, simulate its heating curve, and state the thermal resistance and capacitance you used
Linearise a tank with a square-root outflow at three operating levels and compare each linear model with the full non-linear simulation
Estimate gain and time constant of an unknown plant from a noisy measured step response, then validate the fitted model on a second data set

schedule.title: Transfer functions and block diagrams
schedule.exercise: Reduce a given five-block diagram by hand to a single transfer function and check the result against the simulator.

tasks.title: Convert a second-order differential equation to a transfer function, then list its poles and zeros and mark them on the s-plane
Reduce a block diagram with a nested feedback loop to one closed-loop transfer function and verify it by simulating both forms
Compare the sensitivity of open-loop and closed-loop systems to a 20 percent plant gain error and to measurement noise, and report the trade-off

schedule.title: Time response of systems
schedule.exercise: Predict overshoot and settling time from the pole locations of three second-order systems before running any simulation, then compare.

tasks.title: Measure the time constant of a first-order system from its simulated step response and check it against the transfer function
Design a second-order system with 10 percent overshoot and a 2 second settling time, then verify rise, peak and settling times by simulation
Show when a third pole or a zero can be ignored by comparing the full response with its dominant-pole approximation across several pole positions

schedule.title: Stability and steady-state error
schedule.exercise: Calculate by hand the steady-state error of a type 1 system to step and ramp inputs, then confirm it on the simulator.

tasks.title: Apply the Routh-Hurwitz table to a fourth-order polynomial and state how many poles lie in the right half-plane
Determine the system type and static error constants of a plant, then find the gain that gives under 2 percent ramp error
Specify and tune a controller for a solar-powered irrigation pump to meet overshoot, settling time and steady-state error limits at once

schedule.title: Root locus analysis
schedule.exercise: Sketch a root locus for a given open-loop transfer function by hand using the rules, then compare with the plotted locus.

tasks.title: Plot the root locus of a simple second-order plant and read off the gain at which the poles become complex
Sketch the locus of a third-order plant by hand with asymptotes and breakaway points, then check each feature against the plotted locus
Choose a gain from the root locus to meet 15 percent overshoot and 3 second settling, then show by simulation whether both are met

schedule.title: Compensator design on the root locus
schedule.exercise: Write a design note justifying when you would pick lead, lag or lead-lag compensation, with one example for each.

tasks.title: Add a lead compensator zero to a plant and show on the root locus how the locus bends toward a faster response
Design a lag compensator to cut steady-state error tenfold without disturbing the dominant poles, and verify with a step and a ramp test
Plot root contours for a varying plant parameter and decide the range of parameter values for which the loop meets its specifications

schedule.title: Frequency response and Nyquist
schedule.exercise: Hand-sketch the asymptotic Bode plot of a three-pole plant and check the corner frequencies and slopes against the plotted response.

tasks.title: Plot the Bode magnitude and phase of a first-order lag and read off the corner frequency and the -3 dB bandwidth
Draw the Nyquist plot of a plant with a gain, count encirclements, and use the criterion to decide closed-loop stability
Measure gain and phase margins of a loop, then adjust the gain to give 45 degrees of phase margin and confirm the step overshoot

schedule.title: Frequency-domain design and delay
schedule.exercise: Explain why a time delay reduces phase margin but does not change magnitude, using the delay of a networked loop as the example.

tasks.title: Plot the closed-loop frequency response of a second-order loop and read its resonant peak and bandwidth
Design a lead compensator on the Bode plot to give 50 degrees of phase margin and verify the result with a closed-loop step test
Increase the time delay in a stable loop until it goes unstable, find the critical delay from the margins, and confirm it by simulation

schedule.title: PID control and tuning
schedule.exercise: Write a one-page tuning guide for an operator, explaining what raising each of Kp, Ki and Kd does to rise time, overshoot and noise.

tasks.title: Simulate P, PI and PID control on a first-order-plus-delay plant and compare rise time, overshoot and steady-state error in a table
Tune a PID loop by the Ziegler-Nichols method from the ultimate gain and period, then refine it to cut the overshoot below 15 percent
Tune a DC motor speed loop with anti-windup and a derivative filter so that actuator saturation does not cause large overshoot

schedule.title: State-space methods
schedule.exercise: Convert a third-order transfer function into two different state-space forms and show the two have the same eigenvalues.

tasks.title: Convert a second-order transfer function to state-space form and use the state-transition matrix to compute the state at t equal to 1 second
Test controllability and observability of three given systems using the rank of the test matrices, and explain each result physically
Compute the response of a system from given initial conditions using the matrix exponential and check it against a numerical simulation

schedule.title: State feedback, observers and digital control
schedule.exercise: Capstone problem set: choose a sampling period for a digital PID loop and justify it from the closed-loop bandwidth and the quantisation noise.

tasks.title: Place the closed-loop poles of a second-order plant with state feedback to give 5 percent overshoot and a 1 second settling time
Discretise a continuous PID controller by forward, backward and Tustin methods and compare their step responses at a 20 ms sample time
Implement a digital PID with anti-windup in code, simulate it on a motor model, and find the longest stable sampling period
Model grid frequency as a swing equation with a governor, trip a generator, and choose load-shedding steps that keep frequency above 49 Hz
